Think about that, that's an absurdity and we avoid construing statutes in a way that creates an absurd result. The claimant could be out there doing work. Everybody's getting along, they're doing the right thing and the payment's not even due yet because the work is ongoing and they'd have to sue just because some document was created that says the word punch list on it or just because they're working on components of work that they touched before. But the substantial trivial test fixes that. Trivial work could never take over a year to complete but substantial work could. So that's why substantial work should extend the time to file suit. And this really isn't inconsistent with the existing case law. In the 255 or 713 context, and I've alluded to some of them, but in Excel, it was small items. Those were trivial, they didn't extend the time. In Delta Fire, it was a final walkthrough. In Rickards, there was literally no work. In a different case, I don't have the name of it, but I think Judge Nardella referenced it. There was just three light fixtures that were adjusted. All this to say that we cannot have a statute that was designed to protect subcontractors to do the right thing, interpreted in a way that could literally force them to sue before the payment is due to them. There was this suggestion that Precon got paid for demobilizing. It asked to be paid for demobilizing in the pay application that was unanimously considered wrong. My understanding is that it did not get paid for that work, and that's why we're here. Let's see, with the minute or so I have left, I'll adjust the four-factor test that Ms. Warren has advocated for. And I'll remind you of the Herpel case where the claimant did not intend, once it had installed its work, it did not intend to go home and then come back and then make adjustments and then put it back in, but that's what it did, and it extended the time. In its brief, ARCH only addresses two of the four factors. They don't address whether the work was done in good faith and within a reasonable time. We say Precon satisfies all four. ARCH says, no, you only satisfy two of them. The answers to the four factors are exactly the same here as they are in the Herpel case. They're so similar. So I submit that even if ARCH is right, Herpel suggests that those two factors alone are enough to extend the time. I'll conclude, because the trial court failed to employ the substantial trivial test and instead relied on a mistaken pay application despite an abundance of contrary evidence as to the timing and substantiality of Precon's work. And since Precon's work constitutes the performance of labor under any other circumstance, we ask that you reverse the summary and final judgments in favor of ARCH and on remand, require that summary judgment be granted in favor of Precon on the statute of limitations issue.
